name: Tech Support & Remote Access Scams
summary: A fake technician convinces you your device is infected or that you are owed a refund, then uses remote access to take money directly.

typicalLoss.note: The 'accidental overpayment refund' variant is the most damaging, because the victim voluntarily sends their own money back.

targets: Anyone who has just seen a scary pop-up

howItWorks.detail: A full-screen browser pop-up with sirens and a warning number, or a cold call claiming your machine is sending errors to Microsoft. Neither company monitors your computer this way.
You are guided to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer or similar. This is the moment control is lost, and everything that follows is theatre.
Ordinary system logs are shown as proof of infection, or a command window is used to display alarming but meaningless text.

Either you pay for worthless 'protection', or, in the more expensive version, they claim to have refunded you too much. They edit what you see in your browser to fake the deposit, then ask you to return the difference in cash, crypto or gift cards.

redFlags: An unsolicited call about your computer. Microsoft, Apple and your ISP do not phone you about infections.
A pop-up with a phone number. Real security software never asks you to call anyone.
Any request to install remote access software.
Being asked to log into online banking while someone is connected to your machine.
A refund that requires you to send money back, especially by gift card, crypto or cash.
illustrativeCase: A retired man is called about 'critical errors' from his internet provider. He installs AnyDesk. The technician processes a R500 refund but 'accidentally' types R50 000, and the browser shows the deposit. Distressed and wanting to do the right thing, he transfers R49 500 back. The displayed balance was edited in his browser; no deposit ever occurred.
howToProtect: Never install remote access software because an inbound caller asked you to.
Close alarming pop-ups by force-quitting the browser. Never phone the number displayed.
If someone claims to have refunded you, log out, close everything, and check the balance in your banking app independently.
Agree with older family members that no software gets installed during a phone call, ever.
Remember that money can be shown on a screen without existing. Only your bank's own app is evidence.
ifYouveBeenHit: Disconnect from the internet immediately and uninstall any remote access software.
Change banking and email passwords from a different, clean device.
Phone your bank's fraud line and have accounts monitored or frozen.
Run a reputable security scan, and consider a full reinstall if banking was accessed.

faqs.q: They knew my name and my ISP.
faqs.a: Both are widely available from breached data and directories. Knowing basic details about you is the opening move, not proof of identity.

faqs.q: Can they still access my computer after the call?
faqs.a: Yes, if the software remains installed and configured for unattended access. Uninstall it and check for other new programs.
